assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED is the architecture that turned superconducting circuits into controllable quantum systems: strong coupling of a qubit to a single microwave photon in an on-chip resonator, dispersive readout, and the toolbox on which modern superconducting processors rest. It is original, conceptually clean and has had very broad impact across quantum information and microwave quantum optics.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf, Wallraff and co-authors) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff, Schoelkopf and colleagues) are the decisive steps. Schoelkopf and Wallraff carried the experimental realisation, while Girvin gave the theoretical framework together with Blais. The credit lists four names, so one of Blais or Girvin must be left out, which is a genuine allocation difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of independent confirmation in many laboratories and companies; the interpretation is stable. Recognition would be timely, although the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits raises the question of how closely related recognition should be spaced.
uncertainties: Whether Blais or Girvin should be omitted from a three-person prize is unresolved.

The 2025 prize is in an adjacent area, and the committee might prefer to wait or choose another field. I work in this subfield, so I weigh my own familiarity cautiously and have not independently verified details of priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller proposed the scheme for quantum gates with trapped ions and developed the theory of quantum simulation and quantum-optical control of cold atoms. This created a design framework that experimental groups implemented in ions, atoms and later other platforms, and it is a fundamental contribution to quantum information physics.
assessment.attribution: The 1995 ion-trap gate proposal is a clear joint contribution of two theorists, giving a natural two-person prize. Experimental realisations by others (for example Wineland's and Blatt's groups) are partly recognised by the 2012 prize, which should be taken into account.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally validated for roughly three decades across platforms; the idea is mature and secure, and timing is appropriate.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 Nobel Prize for control of single quantum systems may be argued to dilute the novelty of the recognition.
How the ion-trap gate and the atomic quantum-simulation contributions should be weighted is not clear from the supplied text.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The proposal of spin qubits in quantum dots and their subsequent demonstration, from single-electron spin control to high-fidelity two-qubit gates in silicon, define a leading route to scalable solid-state quantum computing compatible with semiconductor manufacturing. The proposal was original and the experimental follow-through has been steady and significant.
assessment.attribution: Loss and DiVincenzo made the 1998 theoretical proposal and Vandersypen's group delivered key experimental milestones, so a theory-plus-experiment configuration is credible. Other experimental leaders are not in the supplied credit, which leaves a possible allocation gap.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing; silicon spin-qubit fidelities are now high in small devices, but scalability is not yet demonstrated and some may regard recognition as slightly early.
uncertainties: Experimental credit is distributed over many groups and the three-person limit cannot cover it.
Scalable operation of large spin-qubit arrays is still unproven.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error-correcting codes and fault-tolerant computation are what make large-scale quantum computing conceptually possible; Shor's code and Kitaev's topological code and anyon ideas are foundational. The impact on theory and on experimental roadmaps is large and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Shor (first code, fault tolerance) and Kitaev (toric code, topological protection) are leading originators in the credited set; Steane's contribution is also important, and other originators outside the supplied names exist. Credit is broad and difficult to confine to three.
assessment.maturity: The theory is well established, and recent experimental error-correction demonstrations in superconducting and other platforms strengthen the case, but the field is still developing.
uncertainties: Attribution is diffuse among several codes and fault-tolerance results.
A prize for theory may be viewed as more fitting once large-scale logical qubits are demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution links quantum foundations to secure communication; BB84 and the entanglement-based E91 protocol are conceptually deep and original and have led to experiments and commercial systems. It has been a major theme in quantum information science.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) and Ekert (E91) form a conventional trio. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a known priority issue and he is not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature in principle with decades of experimental demonstrations, though practical security and device imperfections remain active topics.
uncertainties: Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea complicates priority.
Part of the field's relevance is practical rather than fundamental physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bringing macroscopic mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state and demonstrating quantum control extends quantum mechanics to visibly macroscopic objects. It is conceptually close to the 2025 prize theme and valuable for quantum technology and sensing.
assessment.attribution: Cleland, Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg are central, but ground-state cooling milestones also involve other groups outside the supplied names, so a three-person prize would leave out significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally well confirmed on several platforms, but the discovery is a compound of milestones and still evolving; recognition is arguably somewhat early.
uncertainties: Compound discovery in which different parts might need different recognition.
Omitted contributors weaken the fairness of the proposed configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical flat bands at the magic angle and the experimental observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened a whole field of moire materials with tunable strong correlations. Conceptual novelty and the rate of subsequent discovery are very high.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the continuum-model prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's group the 2018 experiments, which gives a clean theory-plus-experiment trio; other groups were also influential in the wider moire field.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in many laboratories, though the nature of the superconductivity and correlated states is still debated; recognition may be a little early.
uncertainties: The microscopic mechanism of superconductivity is not settled.
How broadly the wider moire field should be credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength idea, reach fractional frequency uncertainties near 1e-18 and are reshaping time standards, geodesy and tests of fundamental physics. The concept is original and the impact on precision measurement is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye's group delivered leading demonstrations, so a two-person prize is natural; other contributors are plausible but not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent clocks worldwide, with a redefinition of the second under discussion; recognition would be timely, though earlier prizes on frequency combs and ion control partly overlap in subject area.
uncertainties: Overlap in field with earlier recognition in precision spectroscopy and time standards.
Fine details of priority between lattice-clock proposals are not something I have independently verified.
